The Lyman alpha line has a rest wavelength of \(\lambda_0 \approx 1216\) Å. To be detected with optical ground-based telescopes, the observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_0 (1+z)\) must fall within the optical window. The atmospheric cutoff for ground-based optical telescopes is around 3000–3500 Å (near-UV/optical boundary). Using a practical lower limit of \(\sim 3500\) Å:

\[
1+z = \frac{3500}{1216} \approx 2.88 \quad \Rightarrow \quad z \approx 1.88 \approx 1.9
\]

If the line were at a lower redshift, it would fall in the ultraviolet where the atmosphere is opaque. Among the options, 1.9 is the smallest redshift that places the line in the observable optical range.

Answer: D
